# The libraries {#sec-libraries .unnumbered}

Almost nothing in this booklet is written from scratch. Each exercise is mostly
a sequence of calls into libraries other people maintain, and a large part of
learning either language is learning which library owns which job. This page
is the map: what each one is for, where in the booklet you meet it, and where
to read more when the exercise moves faster than you would like.

A note on vocabulary. R calls them **packages** and loads them with
`library(dplyr)`; Python calls them **modules** or **packages** and loads them
with `import pandas as pd` or `from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score`. The
difference matters in one practical way: `library(dplyr)` puts *every* dplyr
function within reach, whereas Python makes you name what you want. That is why
R code reads `filter(...)` and Python code reads `pd.read_csv(...)` — the
prefix tells you where the function came from, and in R you have to remember.

## R

### The tidyverse — getting data into shape

[tidyverse](https://www.tidyverse.org/) is not one package but a family that
shares a design: data frames in, data frames out, verbs that read as English,
and the pipe (`|>` or `%>%`) to chain them. `library(tidyverse)` loads them all
at once; the exercises usually load only the two or three they need, so you can
see which does what.

| Package | What it does | Where you meet it |
|---|---|---|
| [readr](https://readr.tidyverse.org/) | reads `.csv` into a data frame — `read_csv()` | every exercise |
| [dplyr](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/) | the verbs: `filter`, `select`, `mutate`, `group_by`, `summarise`, `arrange` | every exercise |
| [ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/) | plots built by adding layers — `ggplot() + geom_point()` | wherever there is a figure |
| [tidyr](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/) | reshaping between wide and long — `pivot_longer()` | 2.1, 2.3, 5.2 |
| [patchwork](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/) | puts two ggplots side by side with `+` | 2.3 |

The one idea worth carrying away: a dplyr pipeline is a *sentence*. `data |>
filter(age > 60) |> summarise(mean(los))` reads left to right in the order the
work happens, which is why R code in this booklet rarely needs intermediate
variables.

### tidymodels — fitting and evaluating

[tidymodels](https://www.tidymodels.org/) is to modelling what the tidyverse is
to data handling: a family of packages with one grammar. Its central idea is
that *specifying* a model is separate from *fitting* it, and separate again
from *which implementation* does the arithmetic. You will see this in
Exercise 4.1, where the same specification is sent to two different engines.

| Package | What it does | Where you meet it |
|---|---|---|
| [parsnip](https://parsnip.tidymodels.org/) | one vocabulary for many models — `linear_reg()`, `logistic_reg()`, `rand_forest()` | Day 4 onwards |
| [recipes](https://recipes.tidymodels.org/) | preprocessing as a fitted object — `step_normalize()`, `step_impute_mean()` | 2.4, 2.5 |
| [rsample](https://rsample.tidymodels.org/) | splitting and resampling — `initial_split()`, `vfold_cv()` | 2.5, Day 5 |
| [yardstick](https://yardstick.tidymodels.org/) | metrics — `rmse()`, `roc_auc()`, `sens()`, `spec()` | Day 5 |

**Engines.** `set_engine("ranger")` means "fit this random forest using the
ranger package". The specification stays the same; the engine is swapped. Three
engines appear in the booklet and each is a package in its own right:

| Engine | Package | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `"lm"`, `"glm"` | base R | linear and logistic regression |
| `"rpart"` | [rpart](https://cran.r-project.org/package=rpart) | a single decision tree |
| `"ranger"` | [ranger](https://imbs-hl.github.io/ranger/) | random forests, fast |
| `"glmnet"` | [glmnet](https://glmnet.stanford.edu/) | lasso and ridge |

### Specialist packages

| Package | What it does | Where you meet it |
|---|---|---|
| [naniar](https://naniar.njtierney.com/) | visualises missingness — `gg_miss_upset()`, `vis_miss()` | 2.2 |
| [mice](https://amices.org/mice/) | multiple imputation by chained equations | 2.2 |
| [rpart.plot](http://www.milbo.org/rpart-plot/) | draws a readable decision tree | 5.3 |
| [vip](https://koalaverse.github.io/vip/) | variable-importance plots for any model | 9.1 |
| [DALEX](https://modeloriented.github.io/DALEX/) | model-agnostic explanation: break-down, ceteris paribus, partial dependence | 9.3 |
| [DALEXtra](https://modeloriented.github.io/DALEXtra/) | connects DALEX to tidymodels workflows | 9.3 |

## Python

### The scientific stack

| Library | What it does | Where you meet it |
|---|---|---|
| [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/) | the `DataFrame` — `read_csv()`, `groupby()`, `describe()` | every exercise |
| [numpy](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/) | arrays and the maths on them; what pandas is built on | wherever there is arithmetic |
| [matplotlib](https://matplotlib.org/stable/) | plots, built by commanding an `Axes` object | wherever there is a figure |
| [scipy](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/) | scientific algorithms; here `optimize.minimize` | 3.2 |

### scikit-learn

[scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/) is the whole of Days 3 to 9 on
the Python side, and it earns a paragraph of its own because its design is the
thing to learn, not its function names. Every object follows the same contract:
`.fit(X, y)` learns from data, `.transform(X)` or `.predict(X)` applies what was
learned, and `.fit_transform()` does both. Once you know that, a model you have
never seen before is usable in one line.

It is organised into submodules, and the booklet uses nine of them:

| Submodule | What lives there |
|---|---|
| `linear_model` | `LinearRegression`, `LogisticRegression`, `Lasso` |
| `model_selection` | `train_test_split`, `cross_val_score`, `GridSearchCV` |
| `metrics` | `mean_absolute_error`, `roc_auc_score`, `confusion_matrix` |
| `preprocessing` | `StandardScaler`, `MinMaxScaler`, `OneHotEncoder` |
| `pipeline` | `Pipeline` — the object that makes leakage hard to commit |
| `compose` | `ColumnTransformer` — different preprocessing per column |
| `impute` | `SimpleImputer`, `IterativeImputer` |
| `tree`, `ensemble` | `DecisionTreeClassifier`, `RandomForestClassifier` |
| `inspection` | `permutation_importance`, `partial_dependence` |
| `dummy` | `DummyClassifier` — the baseline you must beat |

The [scikit-learn user guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/user_guide.html)
is unusually good: it explains the statistics as well as the code, and is worth
reading for its own sake.

### Specialist

| Library | What it does | Where you meet it |
|---|---|---|
| [shap](https://shap.readthedocs.io/) | Shapley values — what each variable contributed for *one* patient | 9.2 |

## The same job in both languages

| Job | R | Python |
|---|---|---|
| read a csv | `readr::read_csv()` | `pandas.read_csv()` |
| filter rows | `dplyr::filter()` | `df[df.col > x]` or `df.query()` |
| group and summarise | `dplyr::group_by() \|> summarise()` | `df.groupby().agg()` |
| plot | `ggplot2` | `matplotlib` |
| split train/test | `rsample::initial_split()` | `train_test_split()` |
| preprocess without leaking | `recipes` inside a `workflow()` | `Pipeline` + `ColumnTransformer` |
| fit a model | `parsnip` spec `\|> fit()` | `estimator.fit(X, y)` |
| score it | `yardstick` | `sklearn.metrics` |

The pairings are close enough that the hard part is never the translation. It
is remembering that `set.seed(42)` and `random_state=42` do **not** produce the
same split, which Exercise 1.2 makes you prove to yourself.

## If a library is missing

A missing package produces `Error in library(x) : there is no package called 'x'`
in R, or `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'x'` in Python. Install it:

```r
install.packages("naniar")
```

```python
pip install shap
```

Then start a fresh R or Python session — a library installed mid-session is not
always visible to the session that was already running.
